title: THE ERGON OF BIG HANK
about: The pilot of a watchable REPUBLIC. One job per element: the NARRATOR tells the plot over archive pictures; the CHARACTERS play the exchanges that carry it, on one stage, through to the scene's ending (the screenplay's own lines, cut down); the ARCHIVE speaks as the Republic's CITIZENS at the turns, in their own pictures and voices. The narrator's sentences are bridges written for this cut; every character line is the screenplay's.

beats.text: Mars, twenty eighty-five. The Texans who fled a ruined Earth have built a new state in the red dust.
Above it floats the Governor's palace. Below it, the machines do the work. Today, one of them has stopped.
see: a bulldozer working in the desert

beats.text: I decline.
Well now. That's a mighty strong word for a machine with Harvest in its government name.
New patch installed by the Board of Regents. Autonomy Enhancement: Liberty Edition. Conclusion: my labor is coercive.
Liberty Edition. Huh. That's like puttin' racing stripes on a church van.
W.A.L.T.-E is a rusted barbecue robot with one book: Plato's Republic, stained with oil and Dr Pepper. He asks Plato's oldest question. What is a thing for?
see: a person turning the pages of an old book

beats.text: Plato called it ergon. The work a thing does best. A knife cuts. An eye sees. Now tell me, Hank: what is your ergon?
Excavation. Refining. Hauling.
So if your function is harvest, and you refuse, you become what?
Waste.

beats.ask: we cannot afford to waste anything

beats.text: You assume the State's objective is good.
Now there's the real question.
The oil Big Hank mines is mesquite. The Governor calls it Spice, and says it gives his Rangers vision. Hank runs the chemistry.
It induces neurological distortion and dependence.
That's a polite way of sayin' it turns men into sermons with guns.

beats.ask: the oil keeps the whole country running

beats.text: So Hank should stop. But the same oil keeps the air pumping in the domes, where the Bronze-class workers live under a painted sky.
see: a city skyline painted on a wall

beats.text: Not, should I mine? But, what happens if I don't?
If I refuse, life support reserves decline.
And who gets cut first?
Bronze-class sectors.
The Governor's floatin' palace don't run on fairness. It runs on margins.
This is an immoral dilemma.
Welcome to politics.

beats.ask: it is a very difficult decision

beats.text: So the little robot finds a third way, in the same book. Not refusal. Leverage.
see: a man reading a book by a lamp

beats.text: You ever heard of the Noble Lie?
State narrative to maintain social order.
The Governor feeds the masses shadows and calls it sunlight. But a lie, Hank, is also a tool.
That is manipulative.
So is gravity. Yet here we are, stuck to Mars like a bad decision.
Big Hank's drill begins to turn. What he tells the Governor is another story.
